title: India's Pharma Sector, Now Around $60 Billion, Is Projected to Reach $130 Billion by 2030
excerpt: At CPHI India in New Delhi, industry leaders tied the projection to a shift from volume generics to complex generics, biosimilars and innovative therapies — with exports of $30.47 billion in FY2024-25 as the base.
body:
• India's pharmaceutical sector, currently valued at around $60 billion, is projected to reach around $130 billion by 2030, industry leaders said as CPHI India opened in New Delhi on November 23.
  • The growth case rests on a shift from volume-driven generics toward complex generics, biosimilars and innovative therapies, Pharmexcil's director general and Informa Markets India's managing director said.
  • Pharmaceutical exports stood at $30.47 billion in FY2024-25, up 9.4%, according to the Press Information Bureau; around nine free trade agreements covering 38 countries could open roughly $100 billion in potential business, Pharmexcil said.
  • A longer-term ambition of $400 billion by 2047 was cited at the event; the 2030 and 2047 figures are industry and government projections and ambitions, not results.

India's pharmaceutical industry has built its reputation on volume. At the 19th edition of CPHI India, which opened on November 23 at Yashobhoomi in New Delhi, industry leaders made the case that the next phase must be about value — and put numbers on it: a sector valued at around $60 billion today, projected to reach around $130 billion by 2030, according to reporting by Express Pharma from the event.

Raja Bhanu, Director General of the Pharmaceuticals Export Promotion Council of India (Pharmexcil), put the market at $60-70 billion, projected to reach $120-130 billion by 2030, with an ambition of $400 billion by 2047. The Press Information Bureau has likewise described the sector as currently valued at around $60 billion and projected to reach $130 billion by 2030.

What was reported

Pharmaceutical exports stood at $30.47 billion in FY2024-25, registering growth of 9.4% over the previous year, according to the Press Information Bureau. India ranks third globally by production volume. The CPHI exhibition covers active pharmaceutical ingredients, finished formulations, excipients, fine chemicals and natural extracts; its sister event, PMEC India, runs November 24 to 26 at India Expo Mart in Greater Noida and covers machinery, packaging and laboratory systems. Together the two events bring over 2,000 exhibitors and are expected to draw more than 50,000 pharma professionals from over 120 countries, Express Pharma reported.

Where the growth is supposed to come from

Yogesh Mudras, Managing Director of Informa Markets India, said the way forward lies beyond volume-driven generics, in biologics, specialised therapies and complex formulations, and will demand greater investment in innovation, technology, advanced manufacturing and quality systems. Bhanu made the same point on exports: with pharmaceutical exports reaching nearly 200 countries, the focus is shifting from volume-driven generics to higher-value products, including complex generics, biosimilars and innovative therapies.

Trade access is the second lever. Bhanu said India has signed around nine free trade agreements over the past six to seven years, covering 38 countries, with potential business of around $100 billion. Those figures describe opportunity the agreements could open, not trade already booked.

The regulatory side

Dr Chandrashekar Ranga, Joint Drugs Controller (India) at the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO), pointed to revised Good Manufacturing Practices under Schedule M, in effect since January, and said more than 95% of CDSCO's regulatory processes are digital, with a single-window Digital Drug Regulatory System under development. India has reached WHO maturity level 3 for vaccine regulation, with level 4 in more than five regulatory functions, he said. He also credited production-linked incentive schemes with expanding domestic capacity in products where India was earlier import-dependent.

The government's Biopharma SHAKTI initiative, with an outlay of ₹10,000 crore over five years, aims to strengthen India's biologics and biosimilars ecosystem and reduce import dependence, according to the Press Information Bureau.

What to watch next

The projections now have to be earned in the segments leaders named: complex generics, biosimilars and innovative therapies, where approval quality and regulatory speed decide who wins export markets. Export growth — $30.47 billion in FY2024-25 — and the pace at which the free trade agreements convert into actual pharmaceutical trade are the measurable tests of the $130 billion-by-2030 path.
